newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire governor says 2,000 Tutsis surrender.
newsitem.headline: Zaire governor says 2,000 Tutsis surrender.

text.p: Zaire's regional administrator who ordered Tutsis to leave eastern Zaire said on Tuesday about 2,000 had turned themselves in.
Deputy governor Lwasi Ngabo Lwabanji also said he had been reinstated by the central government that declared him suspended for his order against the ethnic Tutsis, called Banyamulenge.

"I have been reinstated today by the central government," Lwabanji told Reuters by telephone from the South Kivu Province capital, Bukavu. He said this was conveyed to him in a telephone call from the deputy interior minister.
There was no immediate government comment.
Lwabanji insisted Tutsis leave their villages in the hills above the town of Uvira or be forcibly evicted, but he toned down his pronouncements against Tutsis.
As a one-week deadline he set for all 200,000 Banyamulenge to leave lapsed on Tuesday, Lwabanji said only those who did not come down from the high plateau would be "exterminated".
That appeared closer to the view of the central government in Kinshasa which, nevertheless, appears powerless to stop regional authorities applying their own tough measures.

The Tutsis immigrated from Rwanda about 200 years ago but have been locked in clashes with indigenous Zaireans who resent their relative wealth. The Zaire army has been drawn into the conflict and is embroiled with fighting armed Banyamulenge.
"For those of them who defy the order and stay in the hills they will be treated as rebels, and like rebels in other countries will be exterminated and expelled," Lwabanji said.
He said 2,000 Banyamulenge had handed themselves in to civilian authorities at a designated reception point at Fizi, 110 km (62 miles) south of Uvira.
Asked what would happen to them, he said: "Zaire welcomes foreigners. It will be up to them to decide whether they stay or go."
"There are some organisations like the Red Cross which will take care of their needs."
Aid workers in the Uvira area contacted by phone from Kinshasa were unable to confirm if Banyamulenge had handed themselves in at the inaccessible town of Fizi.
A spokesman for the International Committee of the Red Cross in Kinshasa said negotiations were in progress to secure a mandate for the ICRC's intervention.
"Our problem is that we have not got adequate security guarantees from either the army or the Banyamulenge which would guarantee our neutrality on the ground," he said.
Lwabanji repeated that a new deadline for Banyamulenge to hand themselves in before they would be treated as rebels was under discussion with the army and would be known in the coming days.
Military and civilian authorities in Kinshasa maintain there is no quit order to Tutsis, but the government's hold on provinces of the vast central African nation is tenuous.

"I know of no operation against the Banyamulenge people as a whole, but certainly the Zairean army will continue operations against those of them who have taken up arms," government spokesman Boguo Makeli said. It is not clear if the government has control of military operations.
